page.line: FEASIBILITY STUDY
Feasibility refers to the practical extent to which a project can be successfully developed
and implemented. A feasibility study evaluates whether the proposed solution is practical,
cost-effective, technically achievable, and beneficial to its intended users. In the case of
Sentinel: An AI-Powered Software Engineering Intelligence and Project Risk Prediction
Platform, this study examines factors such as resource availability, software development
costs, technological requirements, expected benefits, and long-term maintenance needs.
The feasibility study helps determine whether the proposed system is viable before
proceeding with full-scale development.
Conducting a feasibility study for Sentinel involves analyzing the growing need for
integrated software engineering analytics platforms, evaluating existing version control
workflows, and assessing the technological requirements needed to implement AI-
powered risk prediction and repository mining. The study considers development costs,
user adoption, system scalability, security, and future enhancement possibilities. A
comprehensive feasibility study supports informed decision-making and increases the
likelihood of successful implementation.
Types of Feasibility
Economic Feasibility
Technical Feasibility
Behavioral Feasibility
Economic Feasibility
Economic feasibility determines whether the project is financially viable and capable of
providing long-term value. This assessment considers the costs associated with software
development, local or cloud infrastructure, database management, AI model execution,
and system maintenance. It also evaluates the benefits offered to software engineers,
project managers, and technical leads through proactive risk identification and reduced
technical debt.
The economic feasibility study includes the following aspects:
Cost incurred in software development and deployment.
Expenses required for requirement gathering, system analysis, and testing.
Costs associated with local database services and offline AI model execution.
Long-term maintenance and system enhancement costs.
The economic feasibility of Sentinel indicates that the project can be developed using
widely available open-source technologies such as React.js, Node.js, Express.js,
PostgreSQL, and Python, completely eliminating software licensing costs. Because the
machine learning models (XGBoost, LightGBM) and small language models (Qwen2.5 3B
via Ollama) run locally and offline on consumer-grade hardware, there are zero recurring
cloud AI API costs or subscription fees. The system provides substantial value by
reducing manual code review overhead, preventing release delays, and forecasting
engineering risks before they cause costly production failures.
Technical Feasibility
Technical feasibility evaluates whether the required technologies, tools, and resources are
available to successfully develop and maintain the system within the given timeframe and
budget.
The technical feasibility study includes the following aspects:
Evaluating the technical skills and expertise of the development team.
Ensuring the selected technologies are reliable, scalable, and well-supported.
Verifying compatibility between AI components, relational databases, and web
technologies.
Ensuring the system can accommodate future upgrades and enhancements.
Sentinel is technically feasible because it utilizes modern, mature, and well-documented
technology stacks optimized for standard developer hardware (such as an Intel Core i5
processor with 16 GB RAM). The frontend is built using React.js and Tailwind CSS (with
visual components prototyped via Google Stitch), while the backend is powered by
Node.js/Express.js and Python (GitPython) for repository mining. PostgreSQL serves as
the relational feature store for tabular machine learning data, supported by
NetworkX/Neo4j for graph modeling. AI functionalities—such as bug-prone module
prediction, technical debt scoring, SHAP explainability, and natural-language
justifications—rely on locally hosted XGBoost, LightGBM, and quantized Ollama models.
Development is carried out using Visual Studio Code and Git, ensuring efficient
implementation and maintenance.
Behavioral Feasibility
Behavioral feasibility examines how users will interact with the system and whether they
are likely to accept and effectively utilize its features. It focuses on usability, user
adaptability, and overall satisfaction.
The behavioral feasibility study includes the following aspects:
Assessing user acceptance of AI-assisted engineering risk predictions.
Ensuring an intuitive and user-friendly interface.
Providing efficient workflows for software engineers, project managers, and
administrators.
Addressing concerns related to data privacy, metric gamification, and system
reliability.
Sentinel is designed with a clean, role-based interface that prevents punitive individual
tracking (mitigating Goodhart's Law) while giving technical leads and developers
actionable, low-friction insights. Software engineers benefit from localized branch
diagnostics and co-change risks without administrative micromanagement, while project
managers gain objective visibility into sprint delays and architectural bottlenecks. The
platform promotes transparency through Explainable AI (SHAP and natural-language
summaries), making it highly acceptable to development teams.
Feasibility Study Questionnaire
1. How would the organization cope if this system was not implemented? Without
Sentinel, development teams and project managers would continue relying on reactive,
past-facing metrics (such as raw commit counts and open issue totals) or fragmented tools
like SonarQube and GitHub Insights. This reactive posture forces teams to discover
technical debt, bug hotspots, and sprint delays only after they manifest as costly
operational failures and delayed releases.
2. What are the problems with current processes and how would a new system help
alleviate these problems? Current software management processes suffer from a lack of
predictive intelligence and cross-tool cohesion; teams must manually piece together data
from version control, task trackers, and static analyzers. Sentinel alleviates these problems
by providing a unified intelligence layer that automatically mines repositories, predicts
future engineering risks (bugs, technical debt, merge conflicts), explains why the prediction
was made using Explainable AI, and recommends targeted preventive actions.
3. What direct contribution will the system make to the business objectives and
requirements? Sentinel contributes directly by:
Improving software maintainability and reducing long-term technical debt
accumulation.
Predicting bug-prone modules and risky pull requests before code is merged.
Providing mathematically grounded, natural-language explanations for all AI
predictions.
Enhancing sprint planning accuracy and forecasting delivery delays.
Safeguarding team trust by enforcing team-level process aggregation rather than
punitive individual metric tracking.
Offering a centralized engineering health dashboard and automated risk
visualization.
4. Can information be transferred to and from other organizational systems? Yes.
Sentinel is designed with a modular architecture that supports repository integrations
(GitHub, GitLab, and local Git repositories) as well as future issue tracker extensions (Jira,
Azure DevOps, Linear). The platform easily ingests version control metadata and exports
comprehensive reports in CSV and PDF formats.
5. Does the system require technology that has not previously been used in the
organization? Yes. Sentinel incorporates advanced technologies such as software
repository mining, machine learning prediction models (XGBoost/LightGBM), Engineering
Knowledge Graphs, SHAP-based explainability, and local small language models (Ollama).
While these tools may be novel to standard organizational workflows, they are industry-
standard, mature, and run entirely offline on local hardware.
6. What must be supported by the system and what need not be supported? Must
Support:
User authentication and role-based access control (Admin, Manager, Developer).
GitHub and local Git repository integration and parsing.
Repository mining engine for metrics extraction (complexity, churn, commit
frequency).
AI-driven bug prediction and technical debt hotspot identification.
Explainable AI (SHAP feature importance and local LLM natural-language
summaries).
Interactive engineering dashboard with risk heatmaps and health trends.
Need Not Support (Future Enhancements / Main Project Scope):
GitLab, Jira, Azure DevOps, and Jenkins CI/CD pipeline integrations.
Automated merge conflict prediction and sprint delay forecasting.
